item.title: Our Shortage of Psychiatric Care Providers Is Getting Worse
item.description:
Psychiatry

Our Shortage of Psychiatric Care Providers Is Getting Worse

How will the need for psychiatrists change over the next 11 years?

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • The shortage of psychiatrists relative to need will get worse over the next decade.
  • The number of US psychiatrists will decrease from 37,260 FTEs (full-time equivalents) to 32,660 by 2037.
  • The need for psychiatrists will increase from 53,100 FTEs to 76,320 FTEs over this period.
  • Adequacy of the psychiatric workforce is projected to be lowest in the Midwest and South.

by Eugene Rubin MD, PhD and Charles Zorumski MD

Anyone who has tried to make an appointment with a psychiatrist in recent years knows that the wait time is often long, which is an indication that the number of outpatient psychiatrists is probably not adequate to meet the need. To investigate this issue, Jason Silvestre and colleagues examined federal data pertaining to the psychiatric workforce and reported their findings in the journal Psychiatric Services. Their primary objective was “to analyze the supply, demand, and adequacy of psychiatrists serving adults in the United States.”

These investigators analyzed data and projections for 2024 to 2037 from the Health Workforce Simulation Model (HWSM). The HWSM is a project of the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), an agency of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. It is a simulation model using data from various sources, including but not limited to the U.S. Census and the American Medical Association (AMA), to estimate supply and demand of the healthcare workforce.

The Silvestre group defined workforce adequacy as “the ratio of full-time equivalent (FTE) supply to FTE demand.”

Key Findings

In 2024, there were 37,260 full-time equivalent (FTE) psychiatrists serving adults in the U.S. This number is projected to decrease to 32,660 FTEs (12.3%) by 2037. At the same time, there was need for 53,100 FTE psychiatrists in 2024, and this need is anticipated to increase to 76,320 FTEs (43.7%) by 2037. Therefore, workforce adequacy was only 70.2% in 2024, and this is predicted to decrease to 42.8% by 2037.

Of the top 20 medical specialties by number of physicians, the current shortage in the number of psychiatrists relative to need is the most profound. Furthermore, this shortage will substantially increase over the next 11 years, and psychiatry will remain last in terms of workforce adequacy. This problem is likely even worse for subspecialty areas in psychiatry—child and adolescent psychiatry and geriatric psychiatry in particular.

The shortage is most profound in the Midwest and South where workforce adequacy was calculated to be 60% in 2024 and predicted to be under 40% by 2037. In the Northeast, there was no shortage of psychiatrists in 2024, but there could be at least a 35% shortage relative to need by 2037. Not surprisingly, workforce adequacy is lower in nonmetropolitan areas.

One limitation of this study is that it only considered care delivered by psychiatrists. As the authors state, “Further research is needed to understand the roles of mental health therapists and other nonprescribing mental health professionals in bridging the potential gaps identified in this study.”

Thoughts

Over the last decade, the number of U.S. medical and osteopathic school graduates selecting psychiatric residencies has increased substantially. However, the number of available positions in U.S. residency programs has not kept pace and is nowhere near sufficient to counteract predicted shortages.

In addition to the critical shortage of psychiatrists, many practicing psychiatrists do not accept private insurance, Medicare, or Medicaid, further limiting access for patients.

Below we list a variety of strategies that could help provide psychiatric care to the increasing number of patients who need it:

  1. Collaborative care models, in which psychiatrists advise members of primary care teams about managing psychiatric symptoms and disorders in their patients, allowing for psychiatric expertise to reach patients in an efficient manner.
  2. Psychiatric advanced practice nurses and physician assistants, working in collaboration with psychiatrists, can provide direct care.
  3. Better reimbursement by private and public insurance plans might lead to more psychiatrists accepting insurance.
  4. States with the greatest shortage of psychiatrists could develop financial incentives to attract psychiatrists. These states may also benefit from expanding psychiatry residency programs in their states.
  5. Training psychiatrists to focus on treating patients with the most severe disorders would help patients needing the most psychiatric expertise receive care. Psychiatrists could be available in an advisory capacity to non-physician mental health clinicians for patients with less-severe psychiatric disorders.

Psychiatrists have the right to decide whom they wish to treat and which types of insurance to accept. Many practitioners limit their practices to individuals who can afford to pay out of pocket. Unfortunately, due to the shortage of psychiatrists, many patients are unable to access psychiatric care in a timely manner. This problem will likely become dramatically worse over the next decade.

To really provide psychiatric care for those who are sickest, major changes are needed in our healthcare system. Such changes seem unlikely in the near future, and as noted, the problem continues to escalate.

item.title: When Nobody Has to Show Up, How Do We Find Social Connection?
item.description:
Loneliness

When Nobody Has to Show Up, How Do We Find Social Connection?

In U.S. interviews on social connection, no one mentioned obligation. That's the story

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • In our study of social connection, "moral duty or obligation" never appeared in U.S. interviews.
  • U.S. participants described connection as chosen, mutual, and comfortable—but without inherent security.
  • Loneliness was defined less as absence of others than as invisibility: unknown while surrounded by people.
  • Self-reliance recasts loneliness as personal failure, which makes it so hard to discuss.

"Didn't feel like anybody really knew me, even though I was with them and trying."

That is how one U.S. participant described disconnection in our eight-country investigation of social connection, for which we conducted in-depth interviews across Brazil, China, India, Morocco, the Philippines, Türkiye, the United States, and Zimbabwe. In earlier posts in this series, we described how loneliness hides behind Brazil's smile, Turkish hospitality, Filipino cheerfulness, Chinese harmony, and Moroccan togetherness.

While the United States is arguably the country that has done the most to call attention to loneliness, researchers still disagree on how big the problem is; two major 2025 measure U.S. loneliness at roughly 41 percent and roughly 61 percent. That’s a big difference in estimating a big problem. Perhaps it is how loneliness is defined that creates the disparity, or how willing, or unwilling, participants are to report it.

Our 39 U.S. interviews were not designed to estimate the size of the problem. Instead, they asked a different question: What do connection and loneliness actually mean to the people living them? Even more significant than what U.S. participants discussed was what was never named. A glaring omission told a bigger part of the story.

The code that never came up

Every interview across all eight countries was coded against a shared framework. In the U.S. transcripts, one code never appeared: moral duty or obligation. Not once, across 39 long conversations about what makes a relationship good and what makes one fail, did a participant say they kept a relationship because they owed it to someone. Reciprocity and loyalty, as reasons in themselves, also went unmentioned.

What participants described instead was connection as a match. The most common ingredient was sameness—shared values, shared interests, shared humor. Sharing core beliefs, one participant said, "is what breeds that solid connection for me." Another set the bar at ordinary decency: Someone doesn't have to be religious, rich, or poor, "as long as they're nice to other people." A third was more blunt about what happens when a match fails, describing an expectation to get something out of a relationship and to "bail when connection is not fulfilling needs."

This is, in many ways, an appealing model of a social life. It is voluntary and honest, and free of the compulsory togetherness that Moroccan participants described as inescapable. But it has no inherent security or guarantees of presence. When every relationship is chosen, nobody is obliged to notice you.

The absence runs deeper than duty. In India, Zimbabwe, Morocco, and Türkiye, participants routinely described feeling connected to things that are not people: faith, land, ancestors, nation, neighborhood. Chinese participants located belonging in their hometowns. In our U.S. interviews, those referents were largely missing. Belonging was almost entirely interpersonal—specific people, specific reciprocal dynamics.

Faith did appear. Almost half of the U.S. participants mentioned religion or spirituality when describing how they cope with loneliness. But it surfaced as something to reach for once loneliness had already arrived, something that healed, or something that participants turned away from, rather than as a standing source of belonging that made loneliness less likely in the first place.

A lack of connection to something deeper has significant consequences. If your entire connection to the world runs through individual relationships, then a breakup, a move, a death, or a job change doesn't just cost you a relationship, it costs you your infrastructure.

Loneliness as being unseen

So it is not surprising that these participants defined loneliness less as isolation than as invisibility. "That's what loneliness feels like to me, that you're surrounded by activity but not part of it," one said. Another put it directly: It isn't about physical bodies, "it's about appreciation, connection, being seen."

Participants reported feeling lonely alone, in groups, at work, and inside their own families. Several traced their most acute loneliness not to an empty apartment but to a workplace where they didn't fit. The mere availability of people gave no reassurances that being truly seen and known would be possible. And U.S. participants longed to be seen, to be known.

Then the loop closes. If connection is chosen and earned, offering evidence that you are good or worthy of being a part of something, loneliness must indicate that you are unchooseable. Loneliness tells you a story that you are not worthy of connection, and that makes loneliness something to fear, to avoid, to be ashamed of, and to hide.

"We're kind of forced to be…very inward," one participant said. "You're supposed to make something of yourself, and you're not allowed to get any help doing it." Another: "If you're seen as lonely, you're seen as something must be wrong with you." Participants named shame, embarrassment, denial, and a fear of appearing needy. The single most frequent descriptor they used for lonely people was not "sad" but "vulnerable." And in the context of loneliness, vulnerability is painful and scary.

Not everyone agreed. Non-lonely participants named vulnerability as a positive component of their deepest connections. Others said loneliness is simply a common human experience. One participant, when asked if it's hard to discuss, replied: "No, I love talking. I will talk about literally anything."

For measurement, the implication is concrete. U.S. connection lives in chosen families, friendship groups, identity-based communities, and digital ties—none of which are captured by asking who lives in your household or whether you are married. Instruments built on household composition will systematically miss where people from the U.S. actually belong, and systematically miss where they don't.

Each of these eight countries makes loneliness invisible in its own way. Brazil masks it with a smile, the Philippines with cheerfulness, Türkiye with hospitality, China with harmony, Morocco with obligatory togetherness. The U.S. mechanism is different. It doesn't hide loneliness behind warmth. It reassigns it—from a condition of the social world to a verdict on the person. And that makes it less likely to be something anyone will want to report.

And without inherent, obligatory connection, there remains the uncomfortable corollary. In a country where connection is optional, it will not happen by default. It has to be built on purpose.

item.title: Who Pays the Price for ADHD Skepticism?
item.description:
ADHD

Who Pays the Price for ADHD Skepticism?

ADHD skepticism carries unequal costs for certain communities.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Not recognising ADHD does not make its associated difficulties or impairments disappear.
  • How ADHD-related difficulties are understood and responded to is shaped by social and cultural context.
  • ADHD skepticism creates additional barriers for the people least likely to have their difficulties recognised.
Source: Cottonbro Studio/Pexels

In the early 1970s, Dr. Klaus Minde, a German-Canadian child psychiatrist, arrived in Uganda on a WHO secondment. He was looking for something that he did not expect to find—ADHD. At the time, research and clinical understanding of what would become ADHD was dominated by studies of boys in North America and Europe. In Uganda, he established the first child psychiatry clinic in East Africa and began conducting research, including comparative studies on childhood mental disorders in Canada and Uganda.

When publishing his findings, Minde acknowledged that he had approached the research assuming he would not find hyperactive children in Africa. Instead, he was surprised to identify children with similar features to those observed in North America. Drawing on reports from teachers and parents, he identified a subgroup of Ugandan children who showed a pattern of high activity levels with differences in attention and impulsivity, features consistent with those seen in a comparison group of Canadian children. What was different was not the behaviour itself, but how it was understood. In the Ugandan context, these characteristics were more likely to be viewed as nuisances requiring punishment rather than difficulties needing support. As a result, many of these children were not kept in school beyond the first few years.

The boundaries between difference and disorder are inevitably shaped by social context. In that sense, ADHD can be viewed, at least partly, as a social construct. But that does not mean that the characteristics—or the impairments associated with them—disappear when they are not given a medical label.

Earlier this week, a major UK television broadcaster, Channel 4, aired a documentary called The Great ADHD Myth?

Much of the programme's skepticism centred on how commonplace individual ADHD symptoms can sound. But symptoms alone do not make an ADHD diagnosis. Persistence, pervasiveness, and, critically, significant impairment are fundamental to diagnosis.

The programme also gave considerable authority to eminent doctors and psychiatrists, but with the notable exception of ADHD researcher Professor Katya Rubia, many of its most prominent skeptical voices were not specialists in ADHD. Eminence in psychiatry is not synonymous with expertise in ADHD.

Like many psychiatrists of my generation, I started out as an ADHD skeptic. It was skepticism born of ignorance. We had little or no training in it. It is true that in the UK it was rarely diagnosed in children and almost never diagnosed in adults. But as Minde found in Uganda, that doesn’t mean it didn’t exist. That skepticism lasted until I started working with people with ADHD, initially in a specialist national adult ADHD service, later in prisons, and more recently with a large-scale adult ADHD service. I was struck by the significant impairment I encountered and the often dramatic response to treatment.

I am not alone. I recently conducted a qualitative study with consultant psychiatrists working in a UK adult ADHD service, exploring their attitudes towards ADHD diagnosis and treatment. Several described a similar journey, from limited awareness or skepticism to a very different understanding after gaining direct clinical experience of ADHD.

That said, there are legitimate questions to be answered about how to improve ADHD assessment and support. ADHD is associated with well-documented negative outcomes affecting education, work, relationships, physical health, and even life expectancy. Concerns about overdiagnosis coexist with substantial unmet need for ADHD assessment and treatment in the UK. An equally important question may therefore be not simply whether too many people are being diagnosed, but who gets diagnosed—and who does not. Studies have highlighted substantial disparities in access to ADHD care (French et al., 2026).

This is one of the reasons ADHD skepticism and programmes like The Great ADHD Myth? have the potential to be so damaging. Marginalised and ethnic minority communities already face significant barriers to care that include unhelpful stigma and cultural narratives in relation to mental health, including ADHD. These were clearly identified in our qualitative study of Black women’s experiences of adult ADHD diagnosis and care in the UK (Gibbs et al., 2026). Participants described encountering outright disbelief that ADHD existed:

  • “I think from what I observed in the African communities, they don’t think ADHD exists at all.”
  • “When I mentioned it to my friend in university (… .), it was like, ‘Black people don’t have that’.”

Other participants highlighted how increased public awareness and negative portrayals in mainstream and social media had generated a different form of stigma, with ADHD being reframed as a "trend diagnosis" within their communities. Such narratives can create additional barriers to recognising ADHD and seeking or accessing appropriate care and support.

For people in communities where ADHD is already regarded as something that does not exist, or does not happen to people like them, a documentary in which eminent doctors question the diagnosis does not introduce skepticism. It legitimises it.

The question isn't simply whether we risk diagnosing ADHD where it isn't present. We also need to ask who pays the price when ADHD is present and we refuse to see it.

item.title: Your September Sleep Reset
item.description:
Sleep

Your September Sleep Reset

Why sleep regularity matters more than you think.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • In a UK Biobank study of 60,977 adults, sleep consistency predicted mortality risk better than sleep duration.
  • Irregular sleep timing desynchronizes blood pressure, hormone, and immune rhythms.
  • A consistent sleep schedule, supported by small practical changes, can help reset your body clock.

As the relaxing months of summer wind down, do you ever feel a panic when someone asks, “Are you ready for September”? If so, you're not alone. The summer months are glorious. They afford us time with family and friends and allow us to loosen the grip on our otherwise often overstructured days. But as August drifts into September, the need to re-enter a regular routine is ever present. I've experienced this in my own life. As a mother of two young children, I relish the summer months. Our mornings are unhurried, and we aren’t rushing after school to a hundred different activities. But I know what it means when September hits. As a sleep physician and a mom, I’m often caught off guard by the need to return to more organized days and nights.

Getting back into a sleep routine is important, and not just in September. New research shows that how consistent our sleep schedule is may matter more than the total number of hours we sleep each night.

I can recall in my own practice over the years encouraging patients to focus on hitting certain sleep targets. These targets included sleeping between seven and nine hours every night. That's because when you don’t consistently get enough sleep, you can experience real consequences outside of just feeling tired. Insufficient sleep has been linked with cardiovascular disease, Type 2 diabetes, depression, and even a shorter lifespan.

A recent study from the UK of over 60,000 individuals with 10 million hours of sleep data found that greater sleep regularity was associated with a 20 percent to 48 percent lower risk of all-cause mortality and was an even stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration itself. While the study was observational in nature, meaning it can’t prove cause and effect, it does raise the question of whether I, as a sleep physician, should be encouraging my patients to also focus on how regular their sleep is. After reading this study, the answer is an overwhelming yes.

The Importance of the Circadian Rhythm

So why is sleep regularity so important? It has to do with our circadian rhythm. This is an internal 24-hour clock governed by specialized cells deep within our brain. But it's not just our sleep that relies on the circadian rhythm. Many other body systems need a regular 24-hour cycle, too. These include our blood pressure, hormones, and immune function. In fact, disruption to our circadian rhythm can raise our cancer risk by throwing off the daily processes that normally protect our cells.

But I know what you’re thinking because I hear it from my patients frequently. They tell me, “Dr. Filate, I can't go to bed at the same time every night because I won't have any fun!” Now I'm not suggesting that you pull back from social activities and other engagements because of the desire to maintain a strict sleep and wake time, but I want to make sure you understand the importance of maintaining a regular bedtime and wake time as much as possible.

Your September Reset: The “Sept” Method

How do you get back into your routine this September? Start by making small changes first. We know that small changes over time lead to big, sustainable results. To help you, here is my four-step “Sept” method to get your sleep back on track this September:

  • “S”—Set a target wake time. This September, pick your desired wake time and stick to it. For some of you, that may be 6 a.m.; for others it may be 7:30 a.m. Whatever that time is for you, do your best not to deviate from it. There may be mornings when you are exhausted at your wake time. While I know it’s hard, don't stay in bed longer. You can always go to bed earlier that night or squeeze in a short nap in the early afternoon.
  • “E”—Eliminate electronics at night. While challenging, it’s imperative that you try to eliminate electronics and bright light in the hour before bed. Since light is a powerful signal to our circadian rhythm, you want to avoid signaling to your brain that it's morning. If it’s too hard to cut out electronics for 60 minutes before bed, try working through 15-minute increments.
  • “P”—Practice on the weekends too. While it can feel luxurious to relax in bed on the weekends far beyond your usual wake time, this can throw off your sleep routine. You will notice it will be harder to feel sleepy at night. My advice is to try to keep the weekend variability in your sleep schedule to within an hour for both your bedtime and wake time.
  • “T”—Take it outside. When your wake time arrives, it's important to get out of bed and seek outdoor light. As I mentioned, light is the strongest signal for our circadian rhythm, and bright light in the morning will anchor your sleep-wake cycle and will also improve your mood and attention.

As we approach September, I hope my "Sept" method will help you set up a regular sleep schedule. However, the goal here isn’t perfection. Rather, I want you to have the tools to get back into a regular sleep routine. Having a regular sleep schedule will also help you stay as healthy as possible. But I know life isn’t perfect. Some nights I must stay up due to a sick child, a work deadline, or an ailing family member. And that’s OK. The goal here is progress over perfection and knowledge over rigidity. I hope this information and the above tools will help you get back to sleep when the time is right.

item.title: How Important Is the Gut-Brain Axis to Psychiatry?
item.description:
Gut-Brain Axis

How Important Is the Gut-Brain Axis to Psychiatry?

Can we finally put a number on how useful psychobiotics are for mental health?

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Psychobiotics are probiotics that can lift your mood.
  • Studies have been difficult to interpret due to differing protocols.
  • New meta-analyses are attempting to quantify just how beneficial psychobiotics are to psychiatry.

“All life is an experiment. The more experiments you make the better.” –Ralph Waldo Emerson

The gut-brain axis has caught the attention of the world, revealing that our gut plays an intriguing role in our mood and cognition.

But just how large a role? We know that depression and anxiety have numerous causes, including genetics, bereavement, and environmental stress. Those are not microbial problems, but they share a lot of symptoms with a poorly balanced microbiome.

Source: AI-generated with Midjourney

A few years ago, I wrote a book with two of the top researchers of the gut-brain axis, Ted Dinan and John Cryan. They coined the term psychobiotic to refer to substances like probiotics and prebiotics that improve mood and cognition. The book was titled The Psychobiotic Revolution, and it was published by National Geographic. We were all surprised when it became a bestseller. Apparently, we hit a nerve.

At the time, most of Cryan and Dinan’s studies were done in mice, specifically germ-free mice. These are perfect animals for this kind of research, because you could see how different the mice were without any microbes, and then you could introduce microbes to see what changes they made.

Not just mice

My editor and I were worried about the lack of human studies. We were ready to change the title to “What to Do With a Depressed Mouse.” But Cryan and Dinan assured us that human studies were on the way, and they didn’t disappoint. Nevertheless, it has been tricky to pinpoint just how important psychobiotics are to psychological issues like depression, anxiety, bipolar, dementia, and schizophrenia.

Dinan, who is a practicing (and highly sought-out) psychiatrist, was already using psychobiotics with his patients. But it’s hard to tease out how much of the benefit comes from standard therapy and how much from psychobiotics.

So, I was thrilled to see some new meta-analyses that directly tackle the size of the effect of psychobiotics on depression and anxiety.

What is a meta-analysis?

A meta-analysis takes the results of several studies and combines them to give them greater statistical power than any one of them individually. Typically, you weight bigger studies higher because the more subjects you have, the greater the signal-to-noise ratio. Then you average all the weighted studies together. The effectiveness of the intervention is typically measured by the standard mean difference (SMD). As a rule of thumb, if the SMD is -0.2, the effect is small, -0.5 is moderate, and -0.8 represents a large effect (the minus sign means the intervention reduced the symptoms).

A 2024 study looked at 969 people with depression and found an SMD of -0.96 for probiotics, a significant reduction. For 510 people with anxiety, the reduction was -0.59, still a moderate reduction. They found a small effect for prebiotics—the food for probiotics. However, the contributing studies were all over the map in terms of study duration, probiotic formulations, and possible bias.

A more recent 2026 study found an SMD of -0.5 for depression and -0.19 for anxiety. Again, there were inconsistencies across the studies, something that has plagued this field since the beginning. The studies used probiotic doses ranging from millions to almost a trillion. Some were single strains, some were blends. At least three different depression scales were used.

A positive direction

While these results are no cause for jubilation, the direction was overall positive. That held up with imaging studies. A 2026 meta-analysis looked at 10 different imaging studies and found that psychobiotics produced significant changes in the brain that were linked to improved symptoms. They found physical changes to various brain regions that were correlated with faster reaction time, lowered fear response, and better sleep quality.

This year, the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments evaluated the evidence for microbiome interventions in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD). They found that most interventions were well tolerated, with few adverse events. They concluded that “Probiotics may be cautiously considered as third-line adjunctive treatments for MDD.”

Not exactly a ringing endorsement, but a promising start.

This tracks well with Dinan’s experience. Although Dinan has found excellent results with certain psychobiotics like Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria, he is the first to say that psychobiotics are adjuncts, not replacements for standard therapy.

The upshot

It is worth noting that psychobiotics have very few downsides, unlike many antidepressants, which can lead to weight gain, loss of energy, and brain fog. Better yet, many of the beneficial effects of psychobiotics can be derived from a Mediterranean-style diet, rich in veggies and berries (fiber), as well as yogurt, pickles, olives, and cheese (ferments), all of which favor the growth of healthy gut microbes. It is also delicious.

As a psychiatrist, you might want to keep the psychobiotic angle in mind, especially with patients who have gastric issues. As a patient, you could do worse than adopting a few dietary upgrades. Your depression or anxiety may be partly due to a poorly balanced microbiome. Eating better might even lead to a reduction in psychoactive drugs, and that is something to smile about.

item.title: Should Patients Be Co-authors on Research About Them?
item.description:
Education

Should Patients Be Co-authors on Research About Them?

Personal Perspective: Elevating patient voice in peer-reviewed journals.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Lived experience is a form of expertise that can strengthen research.
  • Patient involvement should be meaningful from research conception through to publication.
  • Patient authorship should reflect meaningful intellectual contribution, not tokenistic involvement.
Source: Fauxels/Pexels

By Dr Ava Easton

I've been thinking a lot recently about who gets to own knowledge. It might sound like an odd question, but bear with me.

Throughout my career, I've sat in countless meetings discussing patient-centred research, patient engagement and co-production. I've watched researchers genuinely strive to involve patients more meaningfully than ever before, and that is something to celebrate. We have come a long way.

But then the paper is published. The author list is made up entirely of academics. The patients—the very people whose experiences shaped the research—appear, if they're lucky, in a short acknowledgement at the end.

And I can't help but wonder whether there is something fundamentally inconsistent about that. And I suspect I will have been guilty of this myself during my publishing career.

Let me be clear. I am not suggesting that every patient involved in research should automatically become a co-author. Nor do I think authorship should be awarded because it feels like the right thing to do.

Academic authorship matters. It carries responsibility as well as recognition.

In my book Life After Encephalitis, I recount the story of when I had been writing a book review which was a wife’s account of her husband’s brain injury. In the review, I stated the book was “a great addition to the brain injury literature.” I was asked to change this because I was informed that the term ‘brain injury literature’ was reserved for ‘academic and research-related’ publications. Some months after this, a similar situation occurred when I was co-writing a peer-reviewed paper which included the narrative accounts of patients, and the editor of the journal advised us they could not publish it in its current form because one of the editorial team had said in reference to them, “Some of the descriptions sound like “soap opera.”

I do think we need to ask ourselves some uncomfortable questions.

Have we really recognised lived experience as expertise, or do we still see it as something that sits just outside the academic world?

Expertise comes in many forms

As chief executive of Encephalitis International, I've spent nearly three decades listening to thousands of patients and families rebuild their lives after brain inflammation.

What continually strikes me is that patients often notice things the literature hasn't yet caught up with. They know which symptoms are most disabling. They know which outcomes matter when you return home from hospital. They know which questions their clinician forgot to ask.

More than once, I've watched researchers rethink an interpretation because a patient quietly pointed out, "That's not actually what happens."

That is expertise. Different expertise, certainly, but expertise nonetheless.

Better research happens when we listen properly

I've always believed that research is stronger when patients are involved from the very beginning—not invited to comment once everything has already been decided. Patients help identify the questions worth asking. They challenge assumptions and remind researchers that a statistically significant improvement isn't always meaningful if it doesn't help their recovery or change their daily life.

They help us remember that behind every piece of data is a person trying to get back to work, return to education, rebuild relationships, or remember what they had for breakfast.

Their perspectives make research better.

Should they be authors?

For me, the answer is often yes. However, authorship should never just be symbolic. One of my concerns is that, in our enthusiasm to demonstrate patient involvement, we risk creating tokenistic gestures. Patients deserve far more than being added to an author list to satisfy a funding application or journal expectations.

The standards should remain the same for everyone: if someone has made a substantial intellectual contribution to the research, been part of its conception, helped interpret findings, contributed to writing or critically reviewed the manuscript, then they should absolutely be considered for authorship.

We also need to recognise the barriers

There is also another side to this conversation.

Academic publishing can be intimidating. The language, the review process and the expectations are unfamiliar even for many healthcare professionals.

Some patients live with fatigue, cognitive difficulties or ongoing health problems that make sustained involvement challenging. Others may not wish to become academic authors. In some papers I have published, the patient contributor has requested anonymity for various reasons, including ongoing medico-legal cases. That choice should always be respected.

Rather than lowering expectations, perhaps we should think about lowering barriers. We mentor early-career researchers through the publication process. Perhaps we should offer similar support to patient partners who want to contribute at that level?

Recognition isn't all or nothing

Of course, not every contribution warrants authorship.

Patients who review participant information sheets, advise on recruitment strategies, or contribute to advisory groups have still made important contributions that deserve genuine acknowledgement. Recognition should reflect their contribution honestly, be that as a co-author or in the acknowledgements section.

In conclusion

If we genuinely believe in patient-centred research, then we should be prepared to ask whether our publication practices reflect those values.

Patients should not become authors because we feel sorry for them, nor because a journal or funder expects it. They should become authors when they have earned authorship through meaningful intellectual contribution, the same standard we apply to everyone else.

Perhaps this isn't really about authorship at all. Perhaps it's about respect. Respecting that knowledge doesn't only come from degrees, laboratories, and university departments, but it also from lived experience—surviving an illness that changes your life forever.

We need both forms of knowledge sitting around the same table, and alongside each other on the author list too.

item.title: AI and the Cognitive Loop
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the Cognitive Loop

From Gödel and Hofstadter to the strange loop we now share with artificial intelligence.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Things that refer to themselves can create loops that never fully resolve.
  • These loops show up in math, art, music, and the way we think.
  • AI now joins our thinking, so understanding it means stepping into the loop.
Source: StockSnap / Pixabay

“This sentence is false.”

Take a moment and think about that. It's a simple sentence that creates a very difficult problem. If the sentence is true, then what it says must be correct, which means it is false. But if it is false, then what it says is incorrect, which makes it true again. Around and around we go.

The idea is ancient and commonly associated with Epimenides and his famous statement that “all Cretans are liars.” The modern formulation is cleaner, but the underlying problem is the same. A statement has somehow turned back upon itself. It is making a claim while simultaneously becoming the object of that claim.

For centuries, this could remain an intriguing puzzle of language and logic. Then self-reference found its way into mathematics, and things got much more interesting.

When Mathematics Looked at Itself

In 1931, Kurt Gödel published what is known as the incompleteness theorems, changing how mathematicians understood the limits of systems. Now, this is usually where discussions like this move quickly past some very difficult math and get to the philosophical implications. But Gödel deserves a brief pause—so I beg the indulgence.

(The incompleteness theorem is often used much more casually than it should be, so here is my simplified version. Gödel showed that any mathematical system will contain statements that cannot be proved within that system. Through his use of encoding, mathematics could make statements about itself. One famous construction amounts roughly to, “This statement cannot be proved within this system.” The actual mathematics is actually beyond me, but the point I want to make is that self-reference had revealed a limit from inside the system itself.)

That's a long way from “This sentence is false,” but something fascinating to me connects them. What began as a puzzle about language had become something much more consequential.

Now the story spins forward. Nearly 50 years later, Douglas Hofstadter gave this broader pattern a memorable vocabulary in Gödel, Escher, Bach. Moving among Gödel’s mathematics, M. C. Escher’s impossible images, and Johann Sebastian Bach’s recursive music, he explored what he called “strange loops,” systems that move through different levels and somehow return to themselves.

That book was published in 1979, a technological lifetime ago. And long before a conversation with a large language model could become part of an ordinary afternoon. Today, it's my contention that the loop has another participant.

When AI Entered the Loop

I think it's fair to say that we describe artificial intelligence (AI) as something we use to think. We ask it questions and increasingly use its responses back. But spend enough time working iteratively with a large language model and something more complex begins to happen.

I ask a question. The machine responds. And the loop begins. The response changes how I understand the problem, which changes what I ask next. A few rounds later, I may find myself somewhere new and unexpected with no obvious relationship to my initial intent.

I'm still in control, deciding where the conversation goes and even ends. But it would be incorrect to suggest that the machine had nothing to do with how I got there. Somewhere in that iterative exchange, the nature of the loop itself has changed.

A Different Kind of Loop

The sentence, or prompt, turns back on itself. Gödel showed that mathematics could do something similar. With AI, I believe that something new is happening. A human mind can now examine its own thinking through a computational system that is also participating in that thinking.

I think of this as recursive participation. The human changes the machine's response, and the response changes what the human thinks or asks next. The process continues, but it never quite returns to where it started.

A calculator can perform arithmetic for me, but I generally understand the division of labor. Search can retrieve information without becoming deeply involved in what I subsequently think about it. Generative AI is different because its response can become part of the development of the idea itself. At some point, describing the machine as simply providing answers starts to feel, using a term from Gödel, incomplete.

When the Instrument Enters the Loop

The story takes another curious turn when we begin using AI to understand what AI is doing to us. Researchers can use AI to study AI, and students can ask AI how it might be changing learning. More broadly, any of us can turn to AI to explore if and how technology is changing the way we think. At that point, the instrument has entered the loop—Hofstadter's "eternal golden braid."

This creates an unusual problem of cognitive self-examination. The technology we are trying to understand can now participate in the process through which we understand it. There is almost something Bach-like and contrapuntal about the exchange where one voice changes what the other encounters next and the idea that returns is never quite the idea that entered. Because each exchange alters what comes next, there may be no completely neutral or unbiased position from which to observe the loop once we are acting within it. Perhaps "recursive participation" is a useful name to capture this condition.

So, for now, we humans remain the agent and ultimately decide what to accept or reject. But agency doesn't remove the deeper problem. There's even an echo here of the observer problem in physics. This is when the act of measurement cannot be completely separated from the system being measured. With AI, the parallel is only metaphorical, but the twisting braid (Hofstadter's line) is interesting. The act of examining AI's influence on our thinking may itself become another instance of that influence.

To examine the loop, we may have to enter it.

item.title: Preserving Global Biodiversity Means Getting Over Ourselves
item.description:
Environment

Preserving Global Biodiversity Means Getting Over Ourselves

Michael Caterino shows how we share an extended moral family with other animals.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • He demands a radical reimagining of our responsibilities as a society and argues again human exceptionalism.
  • Any environmental issues struggle to be heard in a political landscape driven by economic messaging.
  • We are undergoing a major extinction event, and we have almost no idea how many species we’re losing.
Source: Cem ARDALI / Pexels

Science, common sense—and, for many people, spirituality—clearly show that life on Earth is a tightly interconnected menagerie of all sorts of beings. Yet, because humans far too often claim that they are not part of this interconnected web and superior to other beings, things often go destructively awry.

But things don't have to be this way, and for this and other reasons, I was pleased to learn of Dr. Michael S. Caterino's new book Under One Canopy: Environmental Ethics and the Tree of Life, in which he challenges readers to acknowledge their kinship with nonhuman life and demands a radical reimagining of our responsibilities as a society to other species and our magnificent, fragile planet. Here's what he had to say about this forward-looking and most important book.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Under One Canopy?

Michael Caterino: There are so many reasons! At a personal level, I am alarmed at the large-scale erasure of wild places from the world. Thinking about the world my grandchildren will inherit is frankly depressing. Our society seems determined to deny any limits or restrictions on growth and consumption, and that is so obviously wrong-headed that I felt compelled to do something.

Why this particular book? In conservation, one of the chief questions is why should we conserve biodiversity? These days it feels like most answers revolve around the value of nature to sustaining people. It is certainly true that we depend on biodiversity for what we eat, breathe, and build with. But the idea that nature might have its own intrinsic value seems to have little popular resonance.

This is exacerbated by the pressing challenges of climate change. Large parts of the world are becoming less habitable. The southwestern U.S. is running out of water. Fires are spreading across several continents. Coastal cities are flooding more frequently. In the popular press, these threats have swamped most concerns for other species, even the charismatic vertebrates that have generally attracted more sympathetic attention.

Source: Clemson University Press/with permission.

As an evolutionary biologist, it is axiomatic that all life on Earth is descended from a common ancestor; we are members of one evolutionary family. Many members of the family may not look much like you and me. But once you peek under the hood, you see remarkable similarities in genetics, biochemistry, and physiology. Far too few people recognize this kinship, and I thought I could help make it more evident.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

MC: I tried to write in a conversational tone, accessible to non-scientists, and I think anyone with an interest in conservation should find it approachable. Nature lovers of all stripes should gain appreciation for their place in the larger scheme. Homeowners and gardeners will learn that not all bugs they encounter mean them harm. Above all, I am writing for voters. Any environmental issues struggle to be heard in a political landscape driven by economic messaging. Yet, biodiversity decline is having real impacts on our livelihoods and well-being. We need to support politicians who won’t accept sacrificing the future for the present.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

MC: I start by summarizing issues impacting biodiversity. From coral bleaching to plastic pollution to pesticide overuse, there are many threats that get insufficient attention. It is generally accepted among conservationists that we are undergoing a major extinction event, and we have almost no idea how many species we’re losing.

One reason these issues are overlooked is our largely anthropocentric culture—people are prone to believe that the world exists for our benefit. Under such a worldview, we needn’t be bothered with ethical concerns for other species. Even among those who recognize our evolutionary origins, there’s still a tendency to believe our dominance over the rest of the natural world is pre-ordained. Similarly, human exceptionalism prevents us from seeing that our own fate is intertwined with that of other species.

Understanding that biology isn’t everyone’s strong suit, I spend several chapters on some basics. I discuss attributes that all organisms share: how we eat, sleep, mate, and die; how we transmit our genes; and how our existence depends on interactions with species around (and within) us. I explore several branches of the tree of life, showing the paths that various lineages have taken.

Much of the ethical philosophy is inspired by Albert Schweitzer, who gets little airtime these days. He promoted a "Reverence for Life," which saw other species as having intrinsic value on the basis of a shared motivation that he called "will-to-live." To me, this seemed a perfect distillation of much of biology, with varied forms of life manifesting their will-to-live in unique ways.

Beyond that, I consider more practical matters. Were we to grant ethical standing to all species, how should it affect our behavior and laws? I discuss the "Rights of Nature" movement, which supports the idea that other species should have legal rights to exist. I think it’s absolutely reasonable that other species should have some recourse (with our representation) to the legal system to preserve their populations and habitats.

Lastly, the book discusses a valid role for spirituality in the effort, aware, as I am, of the battles between evolutionary and religious ideas on humanity’s origins. Theologians like Schweitzer and Thomas Berry were able to reconcile these perspectives. If spirituality is fundamentally about finding meaning in one’s place in the universe, that is entirely compatible with an evolutionary worldview.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

MC: As I became familiar with the environmental ethics literature, I felt there was a large hole where biology should be. Without a firm understanding of the evolutionary underpinnings of life’s unity, the philosophical arguments felt somewhat hollow. I think that filling that gap will help people see their proper place in life’s ecological and ethical systems.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about the interconnectedness of life on Earth, in the skies, and in the water, they will come to appreciate that we are one of the gang and that what we do affects not just other life forms, but us as well?

MC: Absolutely. I think it’s obvious that we are all in this together. The effects we are having on the Earth’s life support systems affect everyone, regardless of where we live or what we believe. We would be wise to protect other species even on the basis of our own flourishing. Going further to recognize that those other lives matter should speed us toward making just decisions.
